'''Old Khmer''' is the oldest attested stage of the [[Khmer language]], an [[Austroasiatic languages|Austroasiatic]] language historically and presently spoken across [[Cambodia]], [[Southern Vietnam]], and parts of [[Isan|Thailand]] and [[Champasak Province|Laos]]. It is recorded in [[Khmer inscriptions|inscriptions]] dating from the early 7th century until the first few decades of the 15th century. Such inscriptions, spanning nearly a millennium and numbering well over a thousand, present one of the most extensive sources of documentation in Southeast Asia.

Old Khmer was written in an early variant of the Khmer script derived from [[Pallava script|Pallava]], a southern variant of [[Brahmi script|Brahmi]], and in turn became the basis of the scripts used for [[Thai script|Thai]] and [[Lao script|Lao]]. Along with Brahmi and Indian influence on Cambodia, Old Khmer saw an influx of [[Sanskrit]] loanwords in the domains of religion, philosophy, and to a lesser extent, politics. Despite this, Old Khmer retained a prototypical Austroasiatic typology in phonology, syntax, and morphology, being [[Minor syllable|sesquisyllabic]], [[Analytic language|analytic]], having a rich system of [[Morphological derivation|derivational affixes]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Jenner|first=Philip N.|date=2010|title=Old Khmer Grammar|url=https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/bitstream/1885/146758/1/611%20Jenner%20and%20Sidwell.pdf|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=}}</ref>

The language is customarily divided into Pre-Angkorian (611–802) and Angkorian (802–1431) stages based on both the date and the distribution of surviving inscriptions, with Pre-Angkorian inscriptions concentrated in the southern regions of Cambodia. After the abandonment of the sites of Angkor as the political centre of the Khmer-speaking polity, the practice of epigraphy decreased in the following centuries but did not disappear, persisting until the 20th century.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bernon|first=Olivier|date=2002|title=L'inscription K. 1212 du Vatt Samrong Ek dans la province de Tra Vinh au Viêt-nam|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272465371|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=}}</ref> However, inscriptions after the 15th century are customarily held to reflect the [[Middle Khmer]] stage of the language.<ref name=":0" />

== Terminology ==
[[File:03-National Museum of Cambodia-nX-1.jpg|thumb|The Sambor Inscription, containing the earliest dateable usage of the numeral [[zero]] as a decimal value. Written in Old Khmer, it is dated to 683 CE, and describes a list of gifts donated to a temple. Found in [[Kratié province]], [[Cambodia]]]]

As an endogenous term referring to the people and language, ក្មេរ៑ ({{transliteration|km|kmér}}, /kmeː/) is attested in inscriptional lists specifying the ethnolinguistic affiliation of personnel attached to temples alongside terms for other ethnic groups, e.g. [[Mon people|Mon]], [[Pearic peoples|Chong]], [[Bru people|Bru]]. Its provenance is unknown, possibly deriving from ''mer'' "chief", "principal" or "mother".<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Sealang Old Khmer Dictionary|url=http://sealang.net/api/api.pl?query=kmer&service=dictionary&language=oldkhmer|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=}}</ref>

== Attestation and history ==
Old Khmer entered into the historical period rather abruptly in 611, with all earlier inscriptions in present-day Cambodia and the Mekong Delta being written in Sanskrit.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Zakharov|first=Anton O.|date=January 2019|title=The earliest dated Cambodian inscription K. 557/600 from Angkor Borei, Cambodia: an English translation and commentary|journal=Vostok (Oriens) |url=https://www.academia.edu/38608096|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|page=66|doi=10.31857/S086919080003960-3 |s2cid=198885161 }}</ref> Even the earliest inscriptions, however, show a high degree of uniformity in orthography, suggesting a period of development prior to the first epigraphic attestation.<ref name=":0" /> Their contents, like later inscriptions, tend to concern legal matters such as land and property, donations to temples, and genealogies and lineages, suggesting a society already deeply entrenched in lower Cambodia. In terms of geography, the earliest inscriptions are concentrated in the southern parts of Cambodia and subsequent inscriptions show a south-to-north dispersal.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Vickery|first=Michael|date=2003|title=Funan Reviewed : Deconstructing the Ancients|url=http://michaelvickery.org/vickery2003funan.pdf|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=|page=125}}</ref>

Due to the primarily legalistic nature of the inscriptions, the surviving corpus of Old Khmer represents only a partial picture of the language. Nonetheless, they provide important documentary evidence of the language's phonology, morphology, and syntax as well as clues about the natural and sociopolitical environments surrounding its speakers.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Jacobs|first=Judith M.|date=1993|title=Pre-Angkor Cambodia: evidence from the inscriptions in Khmer concerning the common people and their environment|url=http://sealang.net/sala/archives/pdf8/jacob1993pre-angkor.pdf|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=}}</ref>

== Influences ==
Like other classical languages of Southeast Asia, Old Khmer was subject to heavy Sanskrit influence. This is especially evident in religious and philosophical concepts and in calendrical numerology, for which Khmer had no equivalents, but sometimes the choice of Sanskrit words over native equivalents were stylistic rather than necessary.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Jacob|first=Judith M.|date=1977|title=Sanskrit loanwords in Pre-Angkor Khmer|url=http://sealang.net/sala/archives/pdf8/jacob1977sanskrit.pdf|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=}}</ref>

== Phonology ==
There is some ambiguity in sound and grapheme correspondence in Old Khmer. In particular, plain plosives /p/ and /t/ are not distinguished from implosive /ɓ/ and /ɗ/, both sets being represented by '''''p''''' and '''''t''''' respectively. Vowels, in particular, show a higher degree of ambiguity. Written '''''a''''' can represent {{IPA|/ɔ/}}, {{IPA|/ɔː/}}, {{IPA|/a/}}, and {{IPA|/aː/}}; '''''ā''''' can represent {{IPA|/a/}}, and {{IPA|/aː/}}; '''''o''''' can represent {{IPA|/oː/}}, {{IPA|/ɔ/}} and {{IPA|/ɔː/}}; and '''''e''''' and '''''ē''''', can represent {{IPA|/e/}}, {{IPA|/eː/}}, /ɛ/, /ɛː/, {{IPA|/ɤ/}}, and {{IPA|/ɤː/}}. Diphthongs /iːə/ and /uːə/ are represented by digraphs '''''ya''''' and '''''va''''' respectively.<ref name=":0" />

== Orthography ==
Pre-Angkorian (611–802) and Angkorian (802–1431) show minor differences in orthography, reflecting perhaps dialectal differences between the south and the north of the country or perhaps just differences in convention. These differences include representations of certain vowels and consonants.
